entry.title: Hybridkultur: Wie viel Homeoffice ist zu viel? – Culture Analytics #5

media:group.media:title: Hybridkultur: Wie viel Homeoffice ist zu viel? – Culture Analytics #5
media:group.media:description:
Mitarbeitende lieben es, Führungskräfte hassen es – das Homeoffice. Okay, das ist reichlich zugespitzt. Fakt ist aber, dass die Möglichkeit, von zu Hause zu arbeiten, in der Corona-Pandemie massiv ausgeweitet wurde. Seither wird in vielen Unternehmen und Behörden darüber diskutiert, wie viel Remote-Arbeit und wie viel On-Site-Präsenz förderlich für Gesundheit, Teamzusammenhalt und Produktivität sind. Wir sprechen mit einer Expertin der ersten Stunde für hybrides Arbeiten in Teams. Josephine Hofmann leitet am Fraunhofer IAO das Team "Zusammenarbeit und Führung“. Im Podcast spricht sie mit uns darüber, wie sie den Boom des Homeoffice und den Umgang damit in den letzten Jahren erlebt hat, welche Auswirkungen er hat und wie man eine gute Zusammenarbeit in hybriden Teams ermöglicht.
Culture Analytics ist der Podcast über die Wissenschaft der Organisationskultur. Mit spannenden Beispielen und praktischen Einblicken rund um das Thema Organisationsentwicklung ist dieser Podcast perfekt für Führungskräfte, HR-Profis und Studierende, die mehr über die Dynamik der Organisationskultur erfahren wollen. Hört rein und erfahrt, wie ihr den Herausforderungen einer sich ständig verändernden Welt erfolgreich begegnen könnt.
Mehr über das Fraunhofer IAO: https://www.iao.fraunhofer.de

entry.title: Sicherheit neu denken, Resilienz stärken: Wie Systeme stabil und handlungsfähig bleiben

media:group.media:title: Sicherheit neu denken, Resilienz stärken: Wie Systeme stabil und handlungsfähig bleiben
media:group.media:description:
Wie können Unternehmen, Kommunen und kritische Infrastrukturen auch in Krisenzeiten handlungsfähig bleiben?
In diesem Video zu den Themenwochen »Sicherheit und Resilienz« geben Petra Gaugisch, Rebecca Litauer und Dr. Heiko Roßnagel Einblicke in aktuelle Herausforderungen und Lösungsansätze rund um Cybersicherheit, Krisenmanagement und organisatorische Resilienz. Sie zeigen, wie Organisationen Risiken frühzeitig erkennen, sich auf Krisen vorbereiten und ihre Widerstandsfähigkeit nachhaltig stärken können.
Jetzt reinschauen und erfahren, wie Sicherheit und Resilienz zum Erfolgsfaktor in einer zunehmend vernetzten und unsicheren Welt werden.

entry.title: Vielfalt als Stärke: So gelingt eine inklusive Unternehmenskultur - Culture Analytics #2

media:group.media:title: Vielfalt als Stärke: So gelingt eine inklusive Unternehmenskultur - Culture Analytics #2
media:group.media:description:
Culture Analytics – der Podcast zur Wissenschaft der Organisationskultur. Leon und Clemens vom Fraunhofer IAO erklären, was starke Organisationskultur ausmacht und wie man sie gezielt verändert. Mit Erfahrungen aus Projekten und Gäst:innen diskutieren sie das Messen und Verändern von Organisationskultur. Für Führungskräfte, HR-Profis, Studierende und alle, die ihre Organisation weiterentwickeln möchten. Schaltet ein für wertvolle Insights!
In unserer zweiten Folge von „Culture Analytics“ setzen wir unseren Selbstversuch fort. Clemens erzählt aus seiner Forschung zur Gestaltung inklusiver Teams und Organisationen. Frei nach Frank Sinatra, „If I can makeit there, I'm gonna make it anywhere“, diskutieren wir, warum Diversity, Equity und Inclusion ein spannendes und prototypisches Thema der Organisationsentwicklung ist. Denn jede:r will ein inklusives Arbeitsklima, aber auf dem Weg dahin ergeben sich kontroverse Gerechtigkeits-Fragen und die Herausforderung, die Einsatzbereitschaft und das Interesse aller Beschäftigten aufrecht zu erhalten.

entry.title: FTQC4NSc 2026 Symposium Recap: Advancing Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for the Natural Sciences

media:group.media:title: FTQC4NSc 2026 Symposium Recap: Advancing Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for the Natural Sciences
media:group.media:description: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences (FTQC4NSc) is an international symposium that brings together leading researchers from quantum computing, quantum chemistry, materials science, and related fields. The event focuses on advances in fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, quantum error correction, and quantum simulation, with the aim of moving quantum computing toward scientifically and industrially relevant applications. This video presents a recap of FTQC4NSc 2026 in Heilbronn. The symposium was organized by flaQship as part of its activities within the Competence Center for Quantum Computing Baden Württemberg (KQCBW), together with the Center for Advanced Systems Understanding (CASUS) and Heilbronn University (HHN). It highlights key topics, discussions, and outcomes from the event. For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, visit: https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc/

entry.title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Scientific Challenges to Apply Quantum Computing in Drug Design

media:group.media:title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Scientific Challenges to Apply Quantum Computing in Drug Design
media:group.media:description:
Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026
Speaker: Dr. Michael Streif (Boehringer Ingelheim)
Abstract: Scientific Challenges to Apply Quantum Computing in Drug Design
Quantum computers hold the promise of outperforming classical systems and are widely regarded as the future of quantum chemistry and drug design. However, realizing this potential in real-world pharmaceutical applications requires addressing a far broader set of challenges than those typically explored – well beyond ground-state energy calculations for single molecules. In this talk, we examine the scientific challenges that must be overcome to make quantum computing a practical tool for drug design. We will share our latest work on fault-tolerant algorithms and discuss strategies for tackling these challenges.
This talk was presented at the Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences Symposium 2026 in Heilbronn.
For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, please visit https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc

entry.title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Imaginary-time evolution in the age of quantum computing

media:group.media:title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Imaginary-time evolution in the age of quantum computing
media:group.media:description:
Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026
Speaker: Dr. Fedor Šimkovic (IQM Quantum Computers)
Abstract: Imaginary-time evolution in the age of quantum computing
Imaginary-time evolution (ITE) is a central framework for computing ground states of quantum systems, with broad applications in condensed matter physics, quantum chemistry, and related fields. Many variants of ITE have been developed, including approaches based on tensor networks and quantum Monte Carlo. On quantum computers, however, a direct implementation of ITE is obstructed by its intrinsically non-unitary character. This challenge has motivated a rapidly growing body of quantum and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms designed to emulate or approximate imaginary-time dynamics. In this talk, Šimkovic will review recent progress in ITE methods for quantum computers and present several of their contributions to this area. He will first discuss an operator-projected formulation of variational quantum imaginary-time evolution, combined with Majorana propagation. He will then describe hybrid stochastic algorithms inspired by auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo and full configuration-interaction quantum Monte Carlo. Next, he will introduce a stochastic implementation of ITE based on quantum signal processing primitives. Finally, he will give a short introduction to the augmented ITE formalism, which can dramatically accelerate convergence relative to standard ITE and may have implications across a broad range of imaginary-time evolution methods.
This talk was presented at the Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences Symposium 2026 in Heilbronn.
For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, please visit https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc

entry.title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Early fault-tolerant resource estimation for ground-state preparation

media:group.media:title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Early fault-tolerant resource estimation for ground-state preparation
media:group.media:description:
Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026
Speaker: Dr. Marius Bothe (Riverlane Ltd.)
Abstract: Early fault-tolerant resource estimation for ground-state preparation via Lindblad simulation
Recent advances in algorithms for simulating Lindblad dynamics have clarified their theoretical potential, yet their practicality in early fault‑tolerant quantum regimes remains uncertain. We address this question by analyzing the single‑ancilla ground‑state preparation algorithm of Ding et al. as a representative and broadly useful test case. This method is appealing due to its relevance to common subroutines such as phase estimation and its use of a low‑overhead dilation construction. We refine the asymptotic resource analysis of the original work by deriving full prefactors and implementing a Qualtran‑based costing framework that estimates gate counts for Lindblad evolution to a specified accuracy. To complement these analytic bounds, we perform extensive circuit‑level simulations of the Hubbard model, an important early fault‑tolerant application, to obtain empirical error behavior and practical convergence times, which are significantly tighter than worst‑case theoretical guarantees. We study symmetry‑preserving mixing operators and further reduce overhead by constructing optimised filter functions that accelerate convergence. Finally, we compile the resulting circuits to fault‑tolerant architecture. Together, these results provide a concrete, architecture‑aware assessment of the feasibility of Lindblad‑based ground‑state preparation in the early fault‑tolerant era, bridging the gap between theoretical constructions and practical implementation.
This talk was presented at the Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences Symposium 2026 in Heilbronn.
For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, please visit https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc

entry.title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Spectroscopy use cases for fault-tolerant quantum computing

media:group.media:title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Spectroscopy use cases for fault-tolerant quantum computing
media:group.media:description:
Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026
Speaker: Dr. Jan Reiner (HQS Quantum Simulations)
Abstract: Spectroscopy use cases for fault-tolerant quantum computing
Finding and realizing productive use cases is a pressing problem for the field of quantum computation. Identifying problems that are both relevant and genuinely better suited to quantum computation than classical alternatives remains a central challenge. Without more compelling, concrete applications, the promise of fault-tolerant quantum computing risks remaining mostly theoretical. I will argue for use cases within the realm of spectroscopy. At its core, spectroscopy probes the response of a quantum mechanical system to external perturbations — a process governed by real-time dynamics. Computing spectral functions therefore requires simulating the time evolution of quantum states, a task that is natural for a quantum computer, yet difficult for classical methods in general. I will show explicit examples of industrially relevant spectroscopy use cases and estimate the applicability of fault-tolerant quantum computing to perform their underlying calculations.
This talk was presented at the Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences Symposium 2026 in Heilbronn.
For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, please visit https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc

entry.title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Rapid Dissipative Ground State Preparation at Chemical Transition States

media:group.media:title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Rapid Dissipative Ground State Preparation at Chemical Transition States
media:group.media:description:
Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026
Speaker: Soumya Sarkar (University of Technology Sydney)
Abstract: Rapid Dissipative Ground State Preparation at Chemical Transition States
Simulating chemical reactions is a central challenge in computational chemistry, characterized by an uneven difficulty profile: while equilibrium reactant and product geometries are often classically tractable, intermediate transition states frequently exhibit strong correlation that defies standard approximations. We present a protocol for dissipative ground state preparation that exploits this structure by treating the reaction path itself as a computational primitive. Our protocol uses an approach where a state prepared at a tractable geometry is propagated along a discretized reaction coordinate using Procrustes-aligned orbital rotations and stabilized by engineered dissipative cooling. We show that for reaction paths satisfying a localized Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) drift condition in the strongly correlated regime, the algorithm prepares ground states of chemical systems with No orbitals to an energy error $ε_E$ with a total gate complexity scaling as $O(N_o^3/ε_E)$. We provide logical resource estimates for benchmark systems including FeMoco, Cytochrome P450, and Ru-based carbon.
This talk was presented at the Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences Symposium 2026 in Heilbronn.
For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, please visit https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc

entry.title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Significantly more efficient Clifford+T synthesis

media:group.media:title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Significantly more efficient Clifford+T synthesis
media:group.media:description:
Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026
Speaker: Dr. Nick Blunt (Riverlane)
Abstract: Significantly more efficient Clifford+T synthesis for small-angle rotations and application to Trotterization
It is well known that arbitrary-angle rotations can be implemented fault-tolerantly to arbitrary precision by compilation to a Clifford+T gate set. This approach is scalable, but is generally understood to have a high overhead of tens of T gates per rotation. In this talk, we will describe our work to reduce the cost of Clifford+T synthesis, and its application to significantly reduce the cost of fault-tolerant Trotterization for chemistry problems. Our main tool to investigate this task is taking probability and quasi-probability mixtures of Clifford+T channels. In particular, we show that the T cost to implement a rotation channel can be reduced significantly for small-angle rotations, and returning to existing angle-independent results in the worst case. This dispels the commonly-stated claim that Clifford+T synthesis has a high overhead independent of the rotation angle, and is particularly impactful for Trotter circuits, which are dominated by small-angle rotations.
Using our results, we show that the T-gate cost of Trotter circuits compiled to Clifford+T gates becomes constant in the limit of small Trotter step sizes, and can be reduced by orders of magnitude even for large step sizes. Our results are also important for early fault-tolerant quantum computers, as they allow rotations to be implemented with shorter Clifford+T sequences, and should allow more straightforward incorporation of error mitigation.
This talk was presented at the Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences Symposium 2026 in Heilbronn.
For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, please visit https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc

entry.title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: A framework for spin-adapted quantum chemistry on quantum computers

media:group.media:title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: A framework for spin-adapted quantum chemistry on quantum computers
media:group.media:description:
Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026
Speaker: Dr. Nathan Fitzpatrick (Quantinuum)
Abstract: A framework for spin-adapted quantum chemistry on quantum computers
Quantum computers promise to transform molecular simulation, but many existing algorithms overlook the powerful role of spin symmetry in chemistry. The Quantum Paldus Transform provides a new framework that makes spin adaptation a built-in feature of quantum computation. At its core, the transform connects two representations of electronic states: the conventional occupation-number basis used in quantum chemistry, and a symmetry-adapted basis that organises states by total spin, particle number, and orbital symmetries. This shift, grounded in mathematical structure known as Paldus duality, allows quantum devices to work directly with spin-pure states – the natural language of chemistry. The benefits are considerable. Spin-free Hamiltonians reduce to block-diagonal, sparser forms, enabling more efficient simulations. The transform itself admits polynomial-cost implementations and even highly compact circuit constructions. Beyond simulation, the framework facilitates efficient preparation of Configuration State Functions (CSFs) and naturally embeds quantum information in decoherence-free subsystems, offering potential protection against certain noise channels. By extending the quantum Schur transform into the fermionic setting, the Quantum Paldus Transform establishes a principled and practical route for exploiting spin symmetry in quantum algorithms. This framework opens new directions for scalable, accurate, and symmetry-aware quantum chemistry algorithms on quantum computers.
This talk was presented at the Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences Symposium 2026 in Heilbronn.
For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, please visit https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc

entry.title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Near-Optimal Quantum Solvers for Stationary PDEs

media:group.media:title: Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026: Near-Optimal Quantum Solvers for Stationary PDEs
media:group.media:description:
Symposium FTQC4NSc 2026
Speaker: Matthias Deiml (University of Augsburg)
Abstract: Bypassing the Condition Number: Near-Optimal Quantum Solvers for Stationary PDEs
We develop a quantum solver for the Poisson equation, a fundamental building block in scientific simulation and a central benchmark for large-scale computational methods. Our algorithm achieves highly favorable scaling: the number of grid points enters the complexity only logarithmically, while the cost of measurement remains linear with respect to the desired accuracy. In the stationary setting, where the absence of time evolution shifts the computational burden to the system’s condition number, achieving near-optimal performance requires specialized techniques. We therefore address the input bottleneck for encoding discretized operators and implement a quantum preconditioning scheme specifically designed to control this condition number. We integrate these components into a coherent end-to-end solver, which maps high-level model parameters directly to quantities of interest, providing a concrete and scalable pathway for quantum PDE simulation.
This talk was presented at the Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing for Natural Sciences Symposium 2026 in Heilbronn.
For more information about FTQC4NSc 2026, please visit https://flaqship.eu/ftqc4nsc
